_comment: What the CI deploy role may do once it has assumed the trust in
github-actions-deploy-role.json.
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name pnsm-github-deploy \
--policy-name pnsm-deploy --policy-document file://deploy/iam/github-actions-deploy-policy.json
Deliberately narrow: push an image, register a task definition, update a
service, invalidate the CDN. It cannot create roles, cannot read secrets,
and cannot touch the biometric key. A pipeline that can grant itself
permissions is not a pipeline, it is an administrator.
GetAuthorizationToken is account-level and cannot be resource-
scoped, so the whole statement is scoped by repository name instead
via the ecr:ResourceTag / ARN pattern applied at the repository.
RegisterTaskDefinition cannot be resource-scoped by AWS; UpdateService
can, and is, so the blast radius of the unscoped call is a task
definition nobody has told a service to use.
iam:PassRole is the permission that turns a deploy role into an
administrator if left unscoped: anyone who can pass ANY role into a
task can run a container as that role. Restricted to the three roles
a PNSM deployment actually passes -- both task roles and the shared
execution role -- and further bound to ECS so none of them can be
passed to Lambda or EC2.
The SPA is uploaded to the web bucket and then invalidated at the
edge. Without the invalidation, index.html keeps being served from
cache and a deploy appears to do nothing for up to 24 hours.
An explicit Deny so that a later, broader Allow -- an AWS managed
policy attached in a hurry, say -- cannot quietly widen this role into
one that can read the HMAC secret or decrypt an employee's face.
Nothing in a deployment needs either.
